items.source: Robert Sinn / Goldfinger Capital
items.title: Talon hole 562C: 9.65m at 70.91% CuEq. Highest-grade Vault Zone hit yet, starting 771m down
items.idea: Drill hole 25TK0562C returned 9.65m of 15.64% Ni, 16.61% Cu, 21.67 g/t Pd, 23.56 g/t Pt, 18.18 g/t Au and 45.82 g/t Ag, which is 35.46% NiEq or 70.91% CuEq, starting at 771.06m. Sinn calls it the best intercept over more than a few meters he has ever seen. It follows a weak update two weeks ago.
items.angle: Grade times width is about 684 CuEq%-meters from one hole. That is the stat for a domestic nickel/PGM story at a time when copper is down more than 20% from its September high (Authers). Depth and continuity matter more than one hole, so this is a watch item for follow-up drilling, not a resource.
items.tweetA: 70.91% copper-equivalent over 9.65 meters. Typical economic copper ore runs under 1%. One hole is still a long way from a mine, but in a tape where copper is down more than 20% from its high, this is the kind of grade that makes the cycle irrelevant. $TLO $TLOFF
items.tweetB: Everyone wants domestic nickel and PGMs until they have to fund a mine 770 meters underground. Grades like this are what make depth affordable. I'm watching whether the next holes show continuity or this was one pod. $TLOFF

items.source: ChinaTalk / Jordan Schneider w/ Chris McGuire & Peter Harrell
items.title: Megaspeed added to the Entity List, but apparently without the foreign direct product rule
items.idea: Chris McGuire read the Commerce listing live on air: Megaspeed, SpeedMatrix and PT Megaspeed are included, but the FDPR appears not to be attached. Without the FDPR, the listing only blocks US-made goods. AI chips are made in Taiwan with US technology, so Megaspeed could in theory still buy them. His verdict: 'God-levels of incompetence.' Peter Harrell reads it as making Megaspeed the scapegoat on the same day Jensen was reinstated.
items.angle: If the FDPR omission is confirmed, the 'crackdown' headline is close to zero-cost for $NVDA's supply chain. A corrected listing with the FDPR is the real event risk. Watch the Federal Register text and any amendment this week.
items.tweetA: Megaspeed is on the Entity List, with no foreign direct product rule attached. AI chips aren't made in America, so a listing without the FDPR controls almost nothing. Read the rule text, not the press release. $NVDA $TSM
items.tweetB: Same day Jensen returns, Commerce lists the smuggler. Optically tough, mechanically toothless. If someone files an FDPR amendment next week, that's when the export-control risk actually reprices.

items.source: ChinaTalk / Jordan Schneider w/ Chris McGuire & Peter Harrell
items.title: Why Nvidia wants a pardon, not just a dropped probe: the 5-year statute of limitations
items.idea: Harrell: export-control violations carry a five-year statute of limitations. If Trump just shelves the DOJ investigation, the next president can reopen it. Only a pardon or a very favorable settlement gives Nvidia final legal resolution. McGuire counts four open investigations: DOJ, an internal review run by Wachtell, Congress, and the press. A Nvidia sales manager in Taipei has already been indicted.
items.angle: This turns 'Jensen is back' into a tail risk on a timer that runs past 2028. Any settlement headline becomes a positive catalyst. A new administration in 2029 is a reopening risk that nobody is pricing into the multiple.
items.tweetA: Statute of limitations on export-control violations: 5 years. Trump's term ends in about 26 months. Shelving a probe isn't immunity, it's a pause button the next president can press. That's why a settlement is the headline to watch. $NVDA
items.tweetB: The market priced Jensen's return as 'risk removed.' The lawyers price it as 'risk deferred to 2029.' Those are very different discount rates.

items.source: ChinaTalk / Jordan Schneider w/ Chris McGuire & Peter Harrell
items.title: House release: 30% of licensed China AI chips went to companies DoD designates as Chinese military companies
items.idea: Per HFAC chair Brian Mast's release of license data through May: 30% of chips the administration licensed to China went to companies the Department of War designates as Chinese military companies, such as Alibaba and Baidu. Entity-listed Inspur appears repeatedly as installer. Nvidia also had a pending license for New Century, part of Alice Huang's network, while shipping to Megaspeed.
items.angle: This is the evidence base the incoming Democratic Congress will use. It raises the odds that 'compelled license denial' legislation replaces the discretionary system, which hurts the China-revenue optionality in $NVDA and $AMD estimates.
items.tweetA: 30% of the AI chips licensed to China went to companies the Pentagon itself lists as Chinese military companies. An entity-listed firm did the installs. This isn't a smuggling story anymore, it's a licensing story, and licensing is the part Congress can rewrite.
items.tweetB: Bulls model China as upside optionality for $NVDA. After the Mast release, I'd model it as a liability that shows up in subpoenas.

items.source: ChinaTalk / Jordan Schneider w/ Chris McGuire & Peter Harrell
items.title: The pending chip bills don't touch smuggling. The next fight is 'compelled license denials'
items.idea: AI Overwatch (stops Blackwell to China), MATCH (stops ASML DUV) and RASA (remote-access authority) don't block licenses to the next Megaspeed or address anti-smuggling. McGuire says the next Congress will need laws that take discretion away from Commerce: 'you shall deny licenses in X, Y, Z circumstances.' Harrell's worry is 'Swiss-cheese' enforcement, with the rule on paper and licenses granted to Nvidia and its neocloud partners anyway.
items.angle: A shift from discretionary to mandatory export denials in 2027 would be a structural change for Southeast Asian neoclouds and Malaysian data centers that are exposed to remote access. Track which bills ride the December NDAA.
items.tweetA: Every chip bill in Congress right now leaves Commerce discretion over who gets licenses. The real regime change is a 'shall deny' statute, and the Jensen episode just wrote its first draft. 2027 is when export controls stop being negotiable.
items.tweetB: Malaysia data-center capex was built on remote-access arbitrage. Rules that compel denials, rather than allowing them, are the existential risk for that model, and it isn't in anyone's capex forecast.

items.source: ChinaTalk / Jordan Schneider w/ Chris McGuire & Peter Harrell
items.title: 'Policy by stock ticker': the selloff drove the reversal, and only 2% of voters want AI to speed up
items.idea: Schneider compares the Jensen U-turn to debt-ceiling fights: policy flips when markets break. He cites a poll in which only 2% of American voters want AI progress to speed up. McGuire expects the reversal to add volatility over months, not dampen it, as investigations ramp. Harrell: 'juicing the stock market is a core objective' and Trump 'TACOs' when stocks fall.
items.angle: This is a political put on the AI trade, struck at whatever level makes the White House panic. NVDA bottomed near 125. But AI is unpopular at 98-to-2, so the put's credibility decays as 2028 approaches.
items.tweetA: There is now an explicit political put on the AI trade. Struck somewhere around $NVDA 125. The problem: only 2% of voters want AI to speed up. A put written by a lame duck on an asset voters dislike has a very short expiry.
items.tweetB: Debt-ceiling playbook, AI edition: flirt with disaster, markets crack, Washington folds. It works until the side writing the put is no longer the one holding the pen. Democrats take Congress in January.

items.source: ChinaTalk / Jordan Schneider w/ Chris McGuire & Peter Harrell
items.title: American state capitalism: a president choosing the CEO of a top-3 US company
items.idea: Harrell: state capitalism is a hallmark of Trump's second term, and some equity-stake tools may make sense, but the president directly picking the CEO of the second- or third-most valuable US company is a sharp departure. The 2008-09 bailouts pushed failed executives out. Here a company tried to clean house and was overruled.
items.angle: Pair with Authers/Divecha (rule-of-law premium) and Parekh (Intel 9.9% stake precedent). If US governance starts to look like EM governance, a US-vs-world valuation premium built on institutions needs a haircut.
items.tweetA: In 2009 Washington pushed bank CEOs out as the price of help. In 2026 it pushed a CEO back in over his own board's objections. Same tool, opposite direction. That's the definition of state capitalism.
items.tweetB: The US premium over EM equities was always partly a governance premium. Every 'national champion' intervention spends some of it. Nobody marks that to market until it's gone.

items.source: TMAD (Trading Mindset & Data)
items.title: S&P +4.7% to 7,237 and this trader took profits: 'still bear-market trading'
items.idea: TMAD sold Friday's buys into Monday's rip because the speed looked like aggressive short covering, and several names were already fading. Bear-tape checklist: VIX touched 40 Friday, former leaders like NBIS damaged far more than the index, weak sessions closing near lows, rallies stalling below prior highs, little follow-through on green days. Open to trading a Thanksgiving/December rally but not sizing up.
items.angle: A useful counterweight to the Goldman/Nomura squeeze notes. The practitioner read is to rent the bounce, not own it. Day-two follow-through is the tell.
items.tweetA: VIX 40 on Friday, S&P +4.7% on Monday. That combination isn't a bull market restarting. It's what a bear-market rally looks like at full volume. Day two tells you who was buying. $SPY $VIX
items.tweetB: Watch the former leaders, not the index. If names like $NBIS that took the worst damage can't reclaim their breakdown levels on a 7% Nasdaq day, the bounce is shorts covering, not longs returning.

items.source: Capital Flows Research
items.title: NVDA Twitter sentiment at its highest level ever, and call/put open interest at historic extremes
items.idea: Capital Flows: NVDA social sentiment hit an all-time high, with call/put OI and volume at historic extremes on massive underlying volume. Their argument is that a name with this much attention needs an extreme informational edge to trade, and insiders aren't talking. They avoid crowded binary coin flips and say macro and factor flows outweigh any single CEO.
items.angle: Record sentiment plus record options OI one day after a +31% move is the setup for vol crush and pin risk into Thanksgiving week. Better to sell premium than chase delta.
items.tweetA: $NVDA social sentiment: highest ever. Options open interest: historic extreme. One day after a 31% move. When everyone holds the same coin-flip, the edge usually goes to whoever sells it to them. Vol sellers are smiling.
items.tweetB: The smartest line I read today: if the whole market is staring at one ticker, you need a huge informational edge to make money on it. Nobody has that edge on Jensen. Trade the second-order names instead.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes (GS Peter Callahan)
items.title: GS desk: Nasdaq 100's best day since the April 2025 tariff pause, yet clients doubt it
items.idea: Goldman TMT specialist Peter Callahan's 'Temperature Check': the NDX had its strongest session since the April 2025 tariff-pause rally, but institutional clients were more interested in questioning its durability than celebrating. Innes notes the historical pattern of such rebounds at turning points is 'not as comforting as it first appears.' Flow detail suggests short covering rather than real long demand.
items.angle: The April 2025 comparison cuts both ways: that rally marked a durable low. The difference is the cause. Tariff relief was policy-wide, while this one hinges on one CEO's employment status.
items.tweetA: Last time the Nasdaq 100 had a day this big was the April 2025 tariff pause. That one marked the low. That rally ran on a policy change. This one ran on a personnel change. I'd want a lot more proof before calling it the same bottom. $QQQ
items.tweetB: The Goldman desk read is the interesting part: biggest up day in 18 months, and clients spent it asking whether it was real. Skepticism at a bounce isn't bearish by itself. It's fuel, if the data cooperates.

items.source: Bloomberg Points of Return / John Authers
items.title: Nvidia added ~$968B in one session, more than JPMorgan's entire market cap
items.idea: Authers: Nvidia's Monday gain of about $968B exceeds JPMorgan's total market cap. Even so, the S&P 500, Nasdaq 100 and even the SOX (NVDA >10% weight) failed to get back to Nov. 17 levels, when Huang had already resigned. Polymarket had given Huang only 18% odds of being the next CEO, and he was still the single most likely candidate.
items.angle: An 18% prior that came true explains the size of the move. But a trillion-dollar gain that can't lift the SOX back to its post-resignation level means the rest of the semis complex is carrying its own damage.
items.tweetA: Nvidia added more market cap in one day than all of JPMorgan is worth. And the semis index still couldn't get back to where it was the day after Jensen resigned. The bounce fixed Nvidia. It didn't fix semis. $NVDA $SOXX $JPM
items.tweetB: Polymarket had Jensen's return at 18%. An 18% event added ~$968B. Do the reverse: the market was implicitly pricing the Jensen key-man discount at roughly $1T. Nobody had that in their DCF.

charts.desc: NVDA's one-day gain vs JPM market cap; indexes still below Nov. 17; SOX, copper, China credit impulse, yuan and the oil-vs-yields charts

items.source: Bloomberg Points of Return / John Authers
items.title: The dollar rose 0.49% on a massive risk-on day, which is the wrong sign
items.idea: DXY gained 0.49% on Monday, when it would normally fall as risk appetite improves. Indexes stayed down for November and below their peaks. Lango: 'massive technical damage,' still below every major support level. George Noble: a board rehiring a CEO 12 days later under White House pressure 'tells you how desperate things really are.'
items.angle: A rising dollar alongside rallying stocks means tighter financial conditions underneath the squeeze. That fits Innes's 'orchestra not playing' and Gave's yields point. Short EM and metals into strength.
items.tweetA: Nasdaq +6.9%. Dollar +0.49%. That's not a risk-on day, it's a dollar-funding day with an equity squeeze on top. When the $DXY and stocks rise together after a crash, I trust the dollar.
items.tweetB: Risk-on days are supposed to weaken the dollar. Monday didn't. Somebody needed dollars badly enough to buy them into the biggest equity rally in 18 months. That's the liquidity story, not Jensen.

items.source: Bloomberg Points of Return / John Authers
items.title: Moral hazard: is tech now 'backed by the full faith and credit of the US government'?
items.idea: Trump said 'we must protect our geniuses' but wouldn't say which tech CEOs qualify. Jean Ergas (Tigress): many will read it as tech carrying the full faith and credit of the US government. Authers compares it to too-big-to-fail, where an implicit guarantee led to demands for much tighter regulation. Arjun Divecha (GMO): the US-EM return gap rests on institutions and rule of law, and this undermines both. Tina Fordham: 'invest where Trump does' as the ultimate safe-haven trade.
items.angle: TBTF-for-tech compresses the tail, which is bullish near term. It also invites bank-style regulation once Democrats control oversight. A sovereign-guaranteed sector should trade at a utility-like multiple over time, not a growth multiple.
items.tweetA: Too-big-to-fail took 15 years to go from 'implicit guarantee' to 'regulated like a utility.' Tech just got its implicit guarantee. The second half of that story is the part nobody's modeling. $NVDA $QQQ
items.tweetB: GMO's Divecha nailed it: the US premium over EM comes from institutions and rule of law. A president reinstating a CEO is the kind of headline you'd discount 20% in an EM. Why not here?

items.source: Bloomberg Points of Return / John Authers
items.title: Copper down more than 20% from its September ATH. China's credit impulse is flat
items.idea: Richard Abbey (in Authers): copper fell more than a fifth from its September record before Monday's reprieve. Drivers: the AI trade implosion, tariff premium gone after the midterms, and a China liquidity crunch. The Bloomberg Economics China Credit Impulse Index is almost flat, breaking the pattern of Beijing priming the pump. Beijing is leaning on bond issuance to hit 'near 5%' GDP, crowding out credit. Yuan strength since late 2025 hasn't lifted demand.
items.angle: Copper has become an AI proxy plus a China-credit proxy. With both legs weak, the Huang bounce in copper is the one to fade. A real China credit pulse is the reversal signal.
items.tweetA: Copper -20% from the September high, and the China credit impulse is flat for the first time in years. Copper used to be Dr. Copper. Now it's half AI-capex proxy, half Beijing-credit proxy, and both halves are sick. $FCX $HG_F
items.tweetB: Beijing used to answer every slowdown with a credit surge. This time the impulse is flat and growth comes from bond issuance instead. That's a regime change for anything priced on Chinese liquidity: metals, AUD, EM.

items.source: Bloomberg Points of Return / John Authers
items.title: Larry Hu's 'Just Enough' rule: Beijing hits growth targets and no more, and the tech selloff matters for 2027
items.idea: Macquarie's Larry Hu: Beijing's 'Just Enough' rule means meeting growth targets but not overshooting. Strong exports mean weaker domestic support. Policymakers will only boost domestic demand when they can no longer rely on exports, which makes the global tech selloff directly relevant to China's 2027 policy path.
items.angle: Counterintuitive trade: a deeper US tech slump raises the odds of real Chinese domestic stimulus in 2027. China consumer names as a hedge against AI capex.
items.tweetA: Here's the irony: the worse the US AI trade gets, the more likely China finally stimulates domestic demand. Beijing only moves when exports stop doing the work. A long China-consumer position is a hedge on the AI trade. $KWEB $FXI
items.tweetB: 'Just Enough' is the most useful two-word model of Chinese policy I've seen. Never overshoot, never surprise. If you're waiting for the bazooka, you're waiting for exports to break first.

items.source: Bloomberg Points of Return / John Authers
items.title: Gave: oil is down $20, yields haven't fallen, and institutions can't buy the dip because they own illiquid PE
items.idea: Louis-Vincent Gave: normally falling oil lifts bonds, freeing money to rotate into risk assets. Oil has fallen about $20/bbl but yields haven't dropped meaningfully, so no relief. Many institutions have swapped long-dated bonds for private equity, private credit, real estate and infrastructure funds, which can't be sold to buy today's dip in equities and commodities.
items.angle: Gave's point is the structural reason dips stay unbought: the liquidity buffer is locked in private markets. Expect secondaries discounts to widen and LPs to be forced sellers of their liquid assets.
items.tweetA: Oil is down $20 and the 10-year still sits near 4.9%. The bond-to-risk rotation that ends most selloffs is broken. And the pension money that used to buy dips is locked in private credit it can't sell.
items.tweetB: The hidden cost of the private-markets boom: when stocks crash, institutions have nothing liquid to rebalance with. The denominator effect now works in reverse.

items.source: Bloomberg Points of Return / John Authers
items.title: NY Fed's Williams declined to rule out successive rate hikes
items.idea: From the Points of Return summary: NY Fed President John Williams declined to rule out successive rate hikes, saying officials must act over time on inflation. This comes days before Wednesday's October core PCE, expected to accelerate to 3.2% y/y (per Innes).
items.angle: A hiking-cycle signal from the Fed vice chair's seat in the middle of an equity crash is the cross-asset risk nobody is pricing into the Jensen bounce. Front-end puts and the dollar are the expression.
items.tweetA: Stocks just had their best day in 18 months. The NY Fed president won't rule out back-to-back hikes. Core PCE Wednesday is expected at 3.2%. One of these markets is wrong about December.
items.tweetB: The Fed put is gone. A Fed that may hike into an equity crash is the anti-put. Monday's rally was a political put replacing a monetary one. Political puts are less reliable.

items.source: Bloomberg Points of Return / John Authers
items.title: Garrity's four governance risks of a 'key-person override underwritten by government assurance'
items.idea: David Garrity (Laidlaw) lists four problems: policy (the code of conduct names personal relationships as a conflict), security (a political assurance isn't a completed counterintelligence review; skepticism from Rep. Bacon to Rep. Krishnamoorthi), credibility (two unanimous votes in opposite directions in two weeks), and political exposure (the assurance is only as durable as the administration). With Democrats controlling Congress and GOP China hawks emboldened, Huang faces months of controversy.
items.angle: Governance risk is now a political-cycle variable. Index and ESG committees and proxy advisers (ISS/Glass Lewis) at the 2027 AGM are the next venue for this fight.
items.tweetA: Two unanimous board votes, opposite directions, 11 days apart. That isn't a board, it's a weathervane. Watch ISS and Glass Lewis at Nvidia's 2027 AGM. That's where the governance bill comes due. $NVDA
items.tweetB: 'A key-person override underwritten by government assurance.' The assurance has an expiry date: January 2029. Jensen's job security now has a political maturity schedule.

items.source: HFI Research (WCTW)
items.title: Double countdown: Iran's oil-sale revenue runs out by mid-December, and ex-US/China crude stocks are near critical
items.idea: HFIR frames US-Iran as attrition. Iran's winter shortages are rated critical for natural gas, electricity, foreign currency and industrial energy, and high for gasoline, diesel, medicines and livestock feed. Revenue from oil sales that started in late June runs out by mid-December. On the other side, global ex-US/China crude inventory is 'half a step' from critical. A cold winter would bring chaos for both sides.
items.angle: Mid-December is a dated catalyst for Iranian escalation or concession. Long-dated call spreads on Brent into January are a cheap way to own the binary.
items.tweetA: Iran's oil revenue clock runs out mid-December. Global ex-US/China crude stocks are half a step from critical. Two countdowns, same month. Oil at $89 Brent is pricing neither. $USO $XLE
items.tweetB: Everyone models the Hormuz war as a military story. HFIR models it as a cash-flow story: whoever runs out of money or inventory first loses. That's a much more tradeable framework.

charts.desc: Kpler Hormuz flow estimates; HormuzStraitTracker loadings

items.source: HFI Research (WCTW)
items.title: Tanker attacks are overstated: 1-2 ships a day and about 2-3 mb/d of real impact
items.idea: Per people in the oil shuttle trade, actual attacks run about 1-2 ships a day, sometimes Suezmax or product tankers rather than VLCCs. Iran's escalation has cut total flows by about 3 mb/d, which matches Kpler, but loadings aren't collapsing. The physical crude market remains bloated, and WTI is back below $80 with Brent at $89.
items.angle: Loading data beats transit data, which is a useful methodological point. The Brent-WTI spread of about $9+ shows the ex-US physical tightness HFIR describes.
items.tweetA: Brent $89, WTI under $80. That's a $9+ spread, which tells you the tightness is outside the US while American crude piles up. The Hormuz trade is a Brent trade, not a WTI trade.
items.tweetB: Twitter says tankers are burning daily. People actually in the shuttle trade say it's 1-2 ships a day, often not VLCCs. Watch loadings, not headlines. The market already figured this out, and that's why crude is falling.

items.source: HFI Research (WCTW)
items.title: Refining margins look like they're bottoming. The product shortage never went away
items.idea: HFIR: the shift in early October from escorting crude tankers to product tankers marked the peak in refining margins, but the product shortage persists. He is seeing signs that margins are bottoming and will turn higher again.
items.angle: Refiners ($VLO, $MPC, $PSX) sold off with the crude complex. If cracks rebound while crude stays soft, margins widen from both ends.
items.tweetA: Crude falling and refining margins bottoming at the same time is the best setup a refiner can get: cheaper feedstock, scarcer product. $VLO $MPC $PSX
items.tweetB: The October switch from crude escorts to product escorts capped crack spreads. It didn't fix the product shortage. If the next escort priority shifts back to crude, cracks rip.

items.source: HFI Research (WCTW)
items.title: Super El Niño points to a warm winter, which could prolong the Iran war
items.idea: HFIR: a colder-than-normal winter would bring chaos for both sides, but Super El Niño tends to foreshadow a warmer-than-normal winter. Mother Nature may indirectly prolong the war by easing pressure on Iran's gas and power shortages and on Western heating demand.
items.angle: A weather-as-geopolitics variable: a warm winter is bearish for natural gas and heating oil, but it extends the conflict duration. Watch NOAA updates as an input to oil risk premia.
items.tweetA: Super El Niño = warmer winter = less pressure on Iran's gas and power crisis = longer war. The weather forecast may be the most important geopolitical input this winter. $UNG $USO
items.tweetB: I didn't expect a climate pattern to show up in a war-duration model, but here we are. A warm winter takes away the deadline both sides were counting on.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes (Asia Wrap)
items.title: NVDA +31.5% (+$952B), NDX +6.9%, SOX +14%, and a leveraged short NVDA product wiped out
items.idea: Innes's tally: Nvidia +31.5%, adding $952B; Nasdaq 100 +6.9%; S&P 500 +4.7%; semis index +14%. One leveraged short Nvidia product was effectively wiped out. His framing: it took the board 11 days to learn that a Jensen-less Nvidia was worth about $5T less across the broader market. Nationwide's Mark Hackett: Nvidia wasn't worth that much less on Friday, nor 30% more on Monday.
items.angle: Math: $952B on +31.5% implies about $3.0T before and $4.0T after. That is still roughly 20% below the ~$5T peak Parekh cites. The bounce reversed the resignation, not the drawdown.
items.tweetA: $NVDA +31.5% = +$952B. Back-solve it and Nvidia is still roughly 20% below its $5T peak. The bounce erased the Jensen discount, not the AI discount. Those are two separate problems.
items.tweetB: A 3x inverse $NVDA product got wiped out in one session. Leveraged single-stock ETPs are now big enough to be the story. Every policy U-turn is a liquidation event for someone.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes (Asia Wrap)
items.title: The trades that didn't light up: gold under $3,650, AUD/JPY under 105.50, and the 10Y near 4.9%
items.idea: Innes was more interested in what didn't move. Gold stayed below $3,650, AUD/JPY (his preferred carry-appetite gauge) stayed under 105.50, and the 10Y yield held around 4.9% before edging lower on oil, not on the Nasdaq. Brent below $90 helps headline inflation but not core. 'The equity market was celebrating the return of its favourite conductor, but the rest of the orchestra wasn't playing the same tune.'
items.angle: Cross-asset non-confirmation is the cleanest test for this bounce. If AUD/JPY clears 105.50 and gold holds, the rally has breadth. Otherwise fade it.
items.tweetA: Stocks had their best day in 18 months. AUD/JPY didn't care. Gold didn't care. Treasuries shrugged. When carry, gold and bonds all refuse to confirm, I trust them over a one-day squeeze. $AUDJPY $GLD $TLT
items.tweetB: My checklist for whether Monday was real: AUD/JPY above 105.50, the 10Y down on growth (not oil), and the dollar weaker. Zero for three so far.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes (Asia Wrap)
items.title: Core PCE Wednesday is expected to accelerate to 3.2% from 3.1%
items.idea: Innes: October core PCE is expected at 3.2% y/y vs 3.1% prior, alongside consumer confidence Tuesday plus spending and revised Q3 GDP Wednesday, ahead of the Fed's December meeting. Lower energy helps headlines, but the effect on core is indirect. A stronger dollar keeps tightening financial conditions for the financing-hungry AI buildout.
items.angle: Combined with Williams not ruling out successive hikes, a 3.2% print or hotter puts a December hike in play. That would hit long-duration AI equities harder than any CEO news.
items.tweetA: Core PCE heading to 3.2% and the Fed talking about successive hikes, in a market that just priced a political rescue. Wednesday matters more than Monday did.
items.tweetB: The AI buildout runs on cheap financing. Core PCE at 3.2%, a rising dollar and a Fed that might hike: that's the real threat to capex, not who sits in Nvidia's corner office.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes (Asia Wrap)
items.title: 'The AI kimono has been opened': circular financing and neocloud returns are unchanged
items.idea: Innes: Huang's return removes a near-term uncertainty but not the concerns about circular financing, the size of capital commitments, or whether frontier labs and neoclouds can earn adequate returns. Washington's direct intervention may add scrutiny. An equity market whose fortunes depend on one executive's employment status is a warning about how concentrated the AI trade has become.
items.angle: Concentration risk is now explicit: one person's job was worth trillions across the index. Equal-weight vs cap-weight is the clean hedge.
items.tweetA: When one man's employment status is worth trillions across the whole index, that isn't a healthy investment cycle, it's a single point of failure. Equal-weight $RSP vs $SPY is the cleanest hedge I know.
items.tweetB: Jensen coming back didn't change a single neocloud's cost of capital or a single lab's revenue. The financing questions are exactly where they were Friday. The price isn't.

items.source: AI-RTZ / Michael Parekh
items.title: How it happened: AG Blanche to Trump to VP Vance to the board, and the interim CEO learned at the last minute
items.idea: Per The Information and Semafor via Parekh: AG Todd Blanche told Trump DOJ had no evidence against Jensen. Vance relayed that to the board. Trump dialed into the Sunday board meeting, and the vote was unanimous. Interim CEO Colette Kress learned at the last minute. Board chair Harvey Jones had told investors six days earlier the board would not bring Jensen back. Trump was briefed late last year that Alice Huang was believed to be a Chinese intelligence asset and took no action.
items.angle: The decision chain went around management, so any SEC or Congressional probe of the decision process now includes the White House. The Dec. 1 House and Dec. 3 Senate dates are the next volatility events.
items.tweetA: Board chair, last Tuesday: we will not bring Jensen back. Board, Sunday, with the President dialed in: unanimous yes. The interim CEO found out at the last minute. Nvidia's governance is now run from Pennsylvania Avenue. $NVDA
items.tweetB: The detail that matters for 2027 headlines: the President was briefed late last year that Alice Huang was believed to be an intelligence asset, and didn't act. That turns a Nvidia story into a White House story, and the Democratic Congress will run that one.

items.source: AI-RTZ / Michael Parekh
items.title: The four 'Blips' framework: each AI governance shock moved the final say closer to Washington
items.idea: Parekh: Blip 1 (2023) was OpenAI's board firing Altman, resolved by a board reversal. Blip 2.0 (June) was export controls forcing Anthropic to suspend its top models for 19 days, resolved by a deal with Washington. Blip 3.0 (September) was Amodei calling for pacing the frontier, resolved by industry self-pacing. The Mega-Blip is a public company's board reinstating its founder after a presidential call. Each resolution came from a different direction, and each moved control closer to Washington.
items.angle: The framework says AI governance risk is migrating from boards to the state. Price AI equities with sovereign risk, the way you would defense primes.
items.tweetA: Four AI 'Blips' in three years. Board fight, export-control deal, industry self-pacing, presidential phone call. Each one moved the final say closer to Washington. AI companies are becoming defense contractors with consumer apps.
items.tweetB: In 2023 a nonprofit board could fire Sam Altman. In 2026 a public board couldn't keep Jensen out. Within three years the power over AI moved from boards to the government.

items.source: AI-RTZ / Michael Parekh
items.title: Scrutiny calendar: House closed session Dec. 1, public Senate Banking hearing Dec. 3, SEC accounting probe, California AG
items.idea: The open fronts: the Wachtell internal investigation continues; the SEC is probing Nvidia's accounting (Reuters via Axios); a closed House session Dec. 1 with GC Tim Teter; a public Senate Banking hearing Dec. 3 with Jensen; a class action in N.D. Cal.; California AG Bonta probing chip/info flows to China and investor disclosure; D&O cover reportedly $800-950M, which protects individuals but not the company. Democrats take both houses in January.
items.angle: Dec. 3 is a binary for NVDA implied vol. The SEC accounting probe is the underpriced item, since it touches revenue quality ($170B neocloud safety net), not just personal conduct.
items.tweetA: Mark your calendar for $NVDA: Dec 1 closed House session, Dec 3 public Senate hearing with Jensen. Also an open SEC accounting probe nobody's talking about. Personal scandals fade. Accounting questions don't.
items.tweetB: D&O cover of $800-950M against a ~$4T market cap. That protects the directors, not the shareholders. Ask who the board was really protecting when it voted twice in 11 days.

items.source: AI-RTZ / Michael Parekh
items.title: A $5T company with ~60 direct reports, no No. 2, no COO, and 'succession' absent from the annual report
items.idea: Parekh: when Jensen resigned he had about 60 direct reports, no No. 2, no president and no COO. The word 'succession' appears nowhere in Nvidia's annual report. The 11-day search turned up a short bench (Arm's Rene Haas signed a new Arm contract meanwhile). Jensen is 63. Expect a real succession plan to top the Jensen 2.0 agenda. The board has created a national security/export control committee and is hiring a first chief compliance officer.
items.angle: The 11-day interregnum was a free stress test: about $1T of key-man value. Naming a COO or president would be a quiet de-risking catalyst that sell-side models will ignore.
items.tweetA: Nvidia: ~$4T market cap, ~60 direct reports to one man, no No. 2, no COO, and 'succession' isn't in the annual report. The market just showed what that key-man risk is worth: about a trillion dollars in 11 days.
items.tweetB: The bull catalyst nobody is modeling: Nvidia names a real COO. It would be the cheapest trillion dollars of de-risking in corporate history.

items.source: AI-RTZ / Michael Parekh
items.title: Family and culture: son-in-law runs neocloud relationships, the daughter worked on Megaspeed, and NYT reports a $1M+ HR settlement
items.idea: Per FT, NYT and WSJ via Parekh: Madison Huang (de facto chief of staff, physical AI marketing) and son-in-law Nico Caprez worked on the Megaspeed relationship. Nico manages many of Nvidia's multibillion-dollar neocloud relationships. Spencer Huang is a robotics product director. The NYT documents decades of humiliation-based management and at least two settlements, including a confidential $1M+ settlement with a former HR head in 2005 (which a spokesman calls fabrications). Employees estimate more than a dozen key executives left because of Madison.
items.angle: The neocloud relationships, which are central to Nvidia's demand funnel and financing, run through a family member now under scrutiny. Any reshuffle there affects CoreWeave-type counterparties.
items.tweetA: The person managing many of Nvidia's multibillion-dollar neocloud relationships is the CEO's son-in-law, who per the FT also worked on Megaspeed. If you own neocloud credit, that sentence matters more than the reinstatement. $CRWV $NBIS
items.tweetB: Nvidia called itself a family business. The new chief compliance officer will have to decide whether a $4T public company can be one. That answer shows up in 2027 org charts.

items.source: AI-RTZ / Michael Parekh
items.title: The Kingmaker's Kingmaker: what does Trump collect? The Intel 9.9% stake precedent
items.idea: Jensen now owes his job to the President, probably through January 2029. Martin Peers (The Information) asks what Trump will want: an equity stake or a board seat. The precedent: in Aug 2025 Trump demanded Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan resign over China ties. Tan stayed and the US government ended up with 9.9% of Intel. The Information reports Trump and Vance see Jensen as key to protecting open-source AI against Anthropic and OpenAI. CNBC reported Trump's accounts traded up to $97.5M in NVDA.
items.angle: A government equity stake in NVDA would be dilutive and change the governance discount. Open-source championing is also a policy tilt against closed-model labs, relevant for Anthropic and OpenAI valuations and their partners.
items.tweetA: Intel, Aug 2025: Trump demands the CEO quit, CEO stays, government ends up with 9.9%. Nvidia, Nov 2026: Trump brings the CEO back. If the pattern holds, the next headline is a stake. $NVDA $INTC
items.tweetB: Buried in the reporting: the White House reportedly wants Jensen back partly to protect open-source AI from Anthropic and OpenAI getting too powerful. Industrial policy just picked a side in the open-vs-closed model war.

items.source: AI-RTZ / Michael Parekh
items.title: Republicans break with Trump: Cotton, Curtis, Cornyn and Ricketts promise oversight and chip bills
items.idea: A rare GOP break (NYT): Sen. Curtis asks who in government weighed in and on what basis. Cotton (Intel chair) says Congress will pass chip export-control bills 'one way or the other,' including his Chip Security Act. Cornyn asks whether the FBI gave Huang a defensive briefing. Ricketts says the reinstatement doesn't excuse testimony. Cramer says the national-security risk passes to the military. Schumer promises the Democrats' 'full power' to investigate. Bills to block Blackwell to China and track chips abroad are in final talks for the December defense bill.
items.angle: Bipartisan pressure makes chip-tracking and Blackwell-ban language in the NDAA far more likely. That is a headline risk for NVDA's China revenue and a positive for chip-security and location-verification vendors.
items.tweetA: When Tom Cotton and Chuck Schumer are both promising to investigate the same Nvidia decision, the chip export bills in the December NDAA just became law in waiting. Price it. $NVDA
items.tweetB: Cornyn's question is the sharpest: did the FBI give Jensen a defensive briefing, and did he ignore it? That one question could be worth more than the whole Mast release.

items.source: Noahpinion / Noah Smith
items.title: Why the New Right is failing: an online movement that never built institutions
items.idea: Noah Smith argues the New Right put its eggs in the Trump presidency rather than a 'long march through the institutions.' He contrasts this with the Federalist Society, which kept the judiciary balanced. Online virality rewards instant gratification. MAGA built 'no Trump Youth League, no community centers'; rally numbers are down. It's 'a fandom,' 'a subreddit.' He extends the critique to the online left too.
items.angle: Political movements without institutions are high-beta: they peak fast and decay fast. For policy forecasting, assume New Right policies (immigration, tariffs) have a short half-life after 2028 unless they are encoded in institutions.
items.tweetA: The Federalist Society took 30 years to reshape the judiciary. The New Right tried to do it in one news cycle. Movements built on virality have the half-life of a meme. Policies built on them may too.
items.tweetB: Noah's best line: MAGA is 'a digital consumption good.' If politics is a consumption good, it has fashion cycles. The policy risk in 2029 is a style change, not just a party change.

items.source: Noahpinion / Noah Smith
items.title: The coalition that won 2024 got attacked: Hispanic and Asian voters swung back in the midterms
items.idea: Trump's 2024 win rested on Hispanic and Asian voters leaving the Dems, the biggest ethnic realignment since Reagan's 'white ethnics.' The New Right then attacked them: Bo French's anti-Indian rants (he lost the Texas Railroad Commission race by ~670,000 votes), and Stephen Miller encouraging racial profiling in ICE raids. Many Hispanic Trump voters swung back in the midterms or stayed home. James Fishback lost a Florida gubernatorial primary to a MAGA-backed candidate by 37 points.
items.angle: This explains the Democratic midterm sweep that now drives the Nvidia oversight story. Policy volatility from Congress in 2027 traces back to this coalition breakup.
items.tweetA: A Texas Railroad Commission candidate lost by ~670,000 votes after running on anti-immigration. The Railroad Commission regulates oil and gas. When the energy regulator race turns on culture war, energy policy gets weird. $XLE
items.tweetB: Reagan turned Italian, Polish and Irish voters into Republicans for a generation. The New Right won Hispanics and Asians in 2024 and lost much of them within two years. Coalition half-life is a political variable worth tracking.

items.source: Noahpinion / Noah Smith
items.title: Musk now calls himself a moderate, the Palantir CEO says he's a Democrat, and young men are drifting from the right
items.idea: Signs of a movement in retreat: Elon Musk, once 'Dark MAGA,' says he's a moderate; Palantir's CEO is calling himself a Democrat; young men's flirtation with the right was ending by 2026, partly through differential turnout. Smith argues the incel-style pitch, that right-wing politics would fix young men's sex lives, couldn't deliver: 'If you couldn't get a date in 2024, you couldn't get a date in 2026 either.'
items.angle: When CEOs of defense and tech companies reposition politically, it is a leading indicator of where they expect contracts and regulation in 2029. Palantir's government revenue mix makes its CEO's realignment a signal.
items.tweetA: The Palantir CEO now calls himself a Democrat. Musk says he's a moderate. CEOs don't reposition on vibes. They reposition on where they think the 2029 contracts come from. $PLTR $TSLA
items.tweetB: Most underrated political datapoint of 2026: young men drifting away from the right. They were the swing demographic of 2024. Consumer brands that leaned into the 'manosphere' should watch this.
